maitland-joint-mobilization.oneLine: Gentle, rhythmic rocking of a joint, graded I to IV by how far into the range you go, chosen by how irritable the patient's pain is.
maitland-joint-mobilization.storyHeadline: The movement stops. But what is really stopping it?
maitland-joint-mobilization.storyScene: A patient turns their neck. Halfway through, pain appears, and the movement stops. Is the joint stiff, the area sensitive, or the movement simply difficult today? Maitland begins by taking that uncertainty seriously. First, find a movement you can test. Then choose a gentle, graded input and see whether anything meaningful changes.
maitland-joint-mobilization.closer: The thumb supplies the question. The patient's movement writes the answer.

kaltenborn-evjenth-mobilization.oneLine: Mobilization that uses joint shape (the convex-concave rule) to pick the glide direction, and traction grades to loosen, take up slack, or stretch.
kaltenborn-evjenth-mobilization.storyHeadline: A joint can feel restricted. Which direction deserves your attention?
kaltenborn-evjenth-mobilization.storyScene: An everyday movement feels blocked, but pushing harder is not a plan. The Kaltenborn–Evjenth approach invites you to think about joint surfaces, the treatment plane, traction and translatoric glide. You choose a direction deliberately, not because it sounds impressive, but because it might help the movement that matters to the patient.
kaltenborn-evjenth-mobilization.closer: The treatment plane is the map. Reassessment is the destination.

mulligan-mobilization-with-movement.oneLine: A sustained joint glide applied by the therapist while the patient performs the movement that normally hurts, aiming for an instant pain-free result.
mulligan-mobilization-with-movement.storyHeadline: What if the painful movement could be tested differently—right now?
mulligan-mobilization-with-movement.storyScene: The patient reaches, squats or turns, and a familiar pain appears. Instead of treating a resting joint and hoping for a change later, Mulligan MWM brings the important movement into the session. A carefully selected accessory glide accompanies the patient's own action. Then you ask the most useful question: did that movement become easier and more comfortable?
mulligan-mobilization-with-movement.closer: A skilled hand can open the door. The patient still has to walk through it.

mulligan-snags-nags.oneLine: Neck and spine glides applied along the facet joint while the patient moves actively (SNAG) or in gentle oscillation (NAG).
mulligan-snags-nags.storyHeadline: A painful neck movement. A different way to explore it.
mulligan-snags-nags.storyScene: Someone looks over their shoulder and stops because the neck feels painful or restricted. NAGs and SNAGs explore whether a carefully directed mobilization, sometimes combined with active movement, can change that familiar complaint. The direction and timing matter—but so does knowing when the response is not good enough to continue.
mulligan-snags-nags.closer: The patient owns the neck turn; the therapist owns the responsibility to stop.

cyriax-deep-transverse-friction.oneLine: Firm, small rubbing strokes across the fibres of a tendon or ligament, applied exactly on the sore spot.
cyriax-deep-transverse-friction.storyHeadline: A tender tendon is asking for judgment, not a harder thumb.
cyriax-deep-transverse-friction.storyScene: A patient points to a painful tendon and asks for something to loosen it. Deep transverse friction is often taught as a precise local technique, but tenderness alone is not a reason to rub harder. First consider tissue irritability, load tolerance and whether the technique adds anything useful to active rehabilitation.
cyriax-deep-transverse-friction.closer: The grip test has better judgment than the therapist's thumb.

muscle-energy-technique.oneLine: A gentle muscle contraction by the patient against your precise resistance, followed by a stretch or movement into the new range.
muscle-energy-technique.storyHeadline: Sometimes the next movement begins with a gentle contraction.
muscle-energy-technique.storyScene: A muscle seems to guard a movement. Forcing it into more range may only create more resistance. Muscle Energy Technique offers a more cooperative starting point: the patient performs a small, controlled contraction against resistance, then relaxes while you reassess the comfortable movement available.
muscle-energy-technique.closer: Less wrestling, more teamwork. That is the whole plot.

strain-counterstrain.oneLine: Finding a tender point, then holding the body in the position of most comfort for about 90 seconds to settle it.
strain-counterstrain.storyHeadline: The tender point hurts. So why move toward comfort instead of stretch?
strain-counterstrain.storyScene: A tender muscle is already sensitive. Strong pressure or stretching may make it more uncomfortable. Strain Counterstrain turns that instinct around: shorten and position the involved tissues toward ease, monitor the tender point and return slowly. It is a quiet technique that demands careful positioning, not force.
strain-counterstrain.closer: The plot twist is comfort—and it is doing actual clinical work.

myofascial-release.oneLine: Slow, sustained pressure or stretch on the tissue envelope (fascia) until it feels like it softens, either into the restriction (direct) or toward ease (indirect).
myofascial-release.storyHeadline: The patient says, 'It feels stuck.' What does that actually mean?
myofascial-release.storyScene: A patient describes pulling, tightness or an area that never seems to relax. Myofascial Release explores how sustained, comfortable manual contact might change symptoms and movement tolerance. But there is a crucial difference between feeling a change and claiming you physically melted adhesions.
myofascial-release.closer: The hands can feel a story. The reach determines its ending.

soft-tissue-mobilization.oneLine: Hands-on strokes, kneading and pressure on muscle and soft tissue to relax it, improve circulation and improve movement.
soft-tissue-mobilization.storyHeadline: A skilled hand does more than press on a painful muscle.
soft-tissue-mobilization.storyScene: A patient comes in with stiff, protective movement. Soft-tissue mobilization may help them tolerate touch and movement, but the strongest treatment is not automatically the deepest. You begin by listening to tissue sensitivity and the patient's feedback, then choose a pressure and movement that can be reassessed.
soft-tissue-mobilization.closer: The real treatment outcome walks out of the room on its own legs.

trigger-point-compression.oneLine: Steady pressure held on a tender knot in a muscle until its pain eases, usually followed by stretching.
trigger-point-compression.storyHeadline: One tender spot. A whole movement affected.
trigger-point-compression.storyScene: Pressing a small region of muscle may reproduce the patient's familiar discomfort. It is tempting to call that spot the entire diagnosis. A better approach is to map the symptoms, distinguish local tenderness from a broader pain problem, and trial controlled pressure only when it is appropriate and tolerated.
trigger-point-compression.closer: One clue can start the case. It rarely closes it.

iastm.oneLine: Using a smooth hand-held tool to stroke and press the soft tissue to find tight areas and improve movement.
iastm.storyHeadline: The tool looks powerful. The clinical reasoning must be stronger.
iastm.storyScene: A metal instrument glides across the skin, and a patient asks whether it is breaking scar tissue. That is a good moment to separate sensation from science. IASTM applies controlled mechanical and sensory input; any benefit should be judged through tolerance, symptoms and function rather than redness or dramatic claims.
iastm.closer: The stainless steel shines. Clinical reasoning has to shine brighter.

neurodynamic-mobilization.oneLine: Gentle movements that slide or lightly tension a nerve so it moves freely and tolerates movement better.
neurodynamic-mobilization.storyHeadline: Why does a tiny change in position send symptoms down the limb?
neurodynamic-mobilization.storyScene: A patient raises a leg, tilts the head or straightens an elbow—and familiar tingling changes. The nervous system is sensitive to movement and surrounding loads, but this does not mean a nerve is physically trapped. Neurodynamic assessment and gentle sliders can help explore symptom behavior without aggressively provoking it.
neurodynamic-mobilization.closer: The nerve is not auditioning for the longest stretch award.

manual-traction.oneLine: A gentle pull that separates joint surfaces to reduce compression and test or calm symptoms.
manual-traction.storyHeadline: Sometimes the revealing movement is the one that takes pressure away.
manual-traction.storyScene: A patient feels discomfort with a particular position. A carefully supported traction or distraction trial may change how that position feels. The technique is not about pulling as hard as possible. It is about screening first, choosing a safe direction and watching whether the patient's symptoms respond.
manual-traction.closer: A gentle pull can ask a useful question. It cannot tow a diagnosis out of thin air.

high-velocity-low-amplitude-thrust.oneLine: A fast, small, controlled thrust at the end of a joint's range, used only after careful screening and supervised training.
high-velocity-low-amplitude-thrust.storyHeadline: The sound grabs attention. The clinical decision should come first.
high-velocity-low-amplitude-thrust.storyScene: A quick thrust and a joint sound can look dramatic. Yet a click does not prove that a bone moved back into place, and silence does not mean failure. HVLA belongs in the hands of trained clinicians who have screened carefully, obtained consent and weighed lower-risk alternatives.
high-velocity-low-amplitude-thrust.closer: Hollywood gets the soundtrack. Rehabilitation needs the outcome.

pnf-manual-techniques.oneLine: Using the patient's own gentle muscle contractions, with your hand resistance, to improve range, strength and control.
pnf-manual-techniques.storyHeadline: The patient moves. Your hands help the movement make sense.
pnf-manual-techniques.storyScene: Reaching, rolling and stepping ask several muscle groups to work together. PNF uses purposeful resistance, direction and sensory cues to support coordinated movement. Instead of memorizing diagonal patterns as choreography, start with a function the patient wants to regain.
pnf-manual-techniques.closer: A diagonal is rehearsal. Daily life is opening night.

fascial-manipulation.oneLine: A system (Stecco) that uses tender points along fascial lines, treated with deep friction, to treat pain and movement problems.
fascial-manipulation.storyHeadline: A point feels important. But does it explain the problem?
fascial-manipulation.storyScene: Some approaches link movement problems to selected fascial points and sequences. Fascial Manipulation gives clinicians a structured way to form and test those ideas. The challenge is to separate a useful clinical response from claims about fascial anatomy or mechanics that remain uncertain.
fascial-manipulation.closer: The treasure is a useful movement, not an invisible knot with a certificate.

active-release-style-soft-tissue.oneLine: Hold a tight spot with your hand while the patient actively moves the muscle from short to long beneath your contact.
active-release-style-soft-tissue.storyHeadline: What happens when the patient moves beneath your contact?
active-release-style-soft-tissue.storyScene: A tender area may behave differently when the patient actively moves through a comfortable range. Active soft-tissue release combines manual contact with movement, creating an opportunity to explore sensitivity, glide and function. The most useful repetitions are controlled, tolerable and connected to a meaningful task.
active-release-style-soft-tissue.closer: It's a duet. If one partner starts shouting, turn the volume down.

manual-lymphatic-drainage.oneLine: Very light, slow skin-stretching strokes that move fluid toward the lymph nodes, done in a set order.
manual-lymphatic-drainage.storyHeadline: For this technique, lighter can be more appropriate than stronger.
manual-lymphatic-drainage.storyScene: A swollen limb may feel heavy and uncomfortable. Manual lymphatic drainage is often misunderstood as deep massage, but the approach uses carefully directed, light skin movements in appropriate patients. Before beginning, the important decisions are the cause of swelling, safety screening and whether specialist management is needed.

scar-mobilization.oneLine: Gentle massage, skin-rolling and stretching of a healed scar so it moves more freely and feels less tight.
scar-mobilization.storyHeadline: The wound has closed. The movement still feels different.
scar-mobilization.storyScene: A healed scar may feel sensitive or less comfortable when the person reaches, walks or bends. Scar mobilization can be considered as one part of graded exposure and functional recovery. The first question is not how strongly to move the tissue, but whether healing is complete and the person can tolerate contact.
scar-mobilization.closer: Healing wrote the first chapter. Don't tear out its pages.

paivm-ppivm-spinal-assessment.oneLine: Hands-on spinal examination: PPIVMs test movement between vertebrae through natural bends; PAIVMs test small glides between them.
paivm-ppivm-spinal-assessment.storyHeadline: A spinal segment feels stiff. Is that enough to call it the problem?
paivm-ppivm-spinal-assessment.storyScene: A clinician feels resistance under the hands and a patient asks which vertebra is out of place. PAIVMs and PPIVMs can contribute to a spinal examination, but segmental palpation is not a stand-alone diagnosis. Their greater value is in testing whether controlled movement changes the patient's familiar symptoms.
paivm-ppivm-spinal-assessment.closer: The thumb can contribute a clue. It cannot deliver the entire verdict.

myofascial-decompression-dry-cupping.oneLine: Using suction cups on the skin to lift the tissue, either held still or moved, to ease tightness and pain.
myofascial-decompression-dry-cupping.storyHeadline: The circular marks are visible. The actual benefit needs measuring.
myofascial-decompression-dry-cupping.storyScene: Cupping is memorable because its marks are easy to see. But visible discoloration is not evidence that toxins left the body or adhesions broke apart. The clinical conversation begins with realistic expectations, informed consent, skin safety and a short trial linked to a movement the patient wants to improve.
myofascial-decompression-dry-cupping.closer: The circle makes a photograph. The retest makes the clinical story.

facilitated-positional-release.oneLine: A short, gentle method: find the neutral position of a tight area, add a small compression, then move toward comfort for a few seconds.
facilitated-positional-release.storyHeadline: Can a few seconds of comfort change what happens next?
facilitated-positional-release.storyScene: When movement is guarded, adding force is not always the most thoughtful first move. Facilitated Positional Release explores a brief position of ease with a carefully selected facilitating input. The technique should stay gentle, comfortable and honest about the limited evidence for its proposed mechanisms.
facilitated-positional-release.closer: Short scene. Long-lasting lesson: measure before you celebrate.

paris-approach.oneLine: A step-by-step orthopedic examination that decides first whether a joint needs mobilizing, stabilizing or something else, then treats and retests.

mckenzie-mdt.oneLine: An assessment system that uses how symptoms respond to repeated movements to guide a self-management exercise plan.

mennell-joint-play.oneLine: Testing tiny involuntary joint movements ('joint play') that you cannot do by yourself, to find out if a joint is blocked.

fascial-distortion-model.oneLine: A model (Typaldos) that sorts pain into six fascial 'distortions', each treated with a specific manual technique.

balanced-ligamentous-tension.oneLine: A very light osteopathic method: hold a joint at the point where its ligaments feel evenly balanced, until the tissue seems to settle.

spencer-shoulder-sequence.oneLine: A seven-step osteopathic sequence of gentle, rhythmic shoulder movements used for stiff shoulders.

still-technique.oneLine: An osteopathic method that moves the tissue into ease, adds a small compression, then guides it through the restriction.

osteopathic-articulatory.oneLine: Slow, rhythmic, repeated joint movements, taken a little further each time toward a stiff direction.

osteopathic-lymphatic-pump.oneLine: Rhythmic pressure on the chest, belly or feet to encourage lymph and fluid movement, used as an adjunct in some settings.

rolfing-structural-integration.oneLine: A structured series of deep soft-tissue sessions aimed at improving posture and movement.

bowen-technique.oneLine: Very light rolling moves on the muscles with built-in pauses; popular but with little strong evidence.

visceral-manipulation.oneLine: Gentle hand pressure on the abdomen to affect the movement of organs and their connective tissue, with limited evidence.

craniosacral-therapy.oneLine: Extremely light touch on the head, spine and sacrum, with claims about subtle rhythms that are not supported by evidence.
